title: Bottle Cap Inspection with Computer Vision
summary: Learn how to use computer vision to verify the integrity of bottle caps on an assembly line.
body_text: James Gallagher , Aarnav Shah Published Aug 6, 2026 • 7 min read SUMMARY A computer vision system can automatically classify bottle caps as properly sealed, loose, or missing before bottles reach packaging, reducing the manual inspection burden on assembly lines. This tutorial walks through collecting and labeling bottle cap images using Roboflow Annotate, training an object detection model, and deploying it on your own hardware with Roboflow Inference. The resulting system flags non-conforming caps in real time and its output can feed downstream rejection logic or defect-rate tracking. Before bottles can be packaged for distribution, inspections must be run to assure the integrity of the bottle cap. If a bottle cap is not properly sealed, it must be rejected before proceeding to packaging and distribution. Computer vision can be used to for bottle cap inspection to identify whether a cap is or is not properly sealed, and check whether there is or is not a cap present on a bottle. Bottle Cap Inspection with AI In this guide, we are going to walk through how to build a bottle cap inspection system that verifies the integrity of a bottle cap. By the end of this guide, we will have a system that can automatically identify whether a cap is sealed. Here is an example of the system running: Without further ado, let’s get started. Step 1: Create a Project First, create a free Roboflow account . Then, go to your Roboflow dashboard. Click the “Create a Project” page to create a project. You will be taken to a page where you will be asked to configure your project. Choose a name for your project. Select “Object Detection” as your project type. Once you have filled out the required fields, click “Create Project”. Step 2: Upload Bottle Cap Data To build a computer vision system, you need to label images with objects of interest. We need to train our system to identify whether a bottle cap is or is not properly sealed. For that, we will need images that show a bottle cap that is both sealed, not properly sealed, and missing. For optimal performance, we recommend gathering images of bottle caps from your assembly line. Here are a few example images of bottles with different caps: Left: A bottle with an unsealed cap. Right: A bottle with a properly sealed cap. We recommend collecting 20-50 images that show all types of defects you want to identify for your first model. For this example, we have collected images that show: A sealed cap; A loose cap, and; A missing cap. Once you have created a project, you will be taken to a page on which you can upload your data. To upload data, drag images onto the upload data page. Your images will be processed in your browser. Use the images from this dataset if you don't want to collect your own . Then, click “Save and Continue” to upload your images. Step 3: Label Bottle Cap Images The images we uploaded from this dataset had annotations already made to them. To annotate new images, drop them into your project, open Annotate from the left sidebar, and select them. This process is also known as labeling. To create a label, first press “b” on your keyboard or click the box tool in the right sidebar. This will toggle the bounding box tool for use in drawing object detection labels. Click where you want to start drawing your label on the image then drag your cursor around the object of interest. When you have surrounded the region of interest – a full or loose cap – with a box, stop clicking. You can then select a class to assign to your label. Label all bottle caps in the images you uploaded to Roboflow. Step 4: Generate a Dataset Version With all of the images labeled, you can generate a dataset version. A dataset version is a snapshot of your labeled images. You can apply preprocessing and augmentation steps to prepare your model for training and improve model performance, respectively. To generate a dataset, click “Generate” in the sidebar. You will be taken to a page on which you can configure your dataset version. For your first dataset version, we recommend leaving the preprocessing steps as the default. We recommend applying the following augmentations for your first version: Greyscale Noise (up to 1% of pixels) You should only apply a greyscale augmentation if bottle cap color does not matter. If you need to verify the color of a bottle cap, do not apply a greyscale augmentation. Click the “Create” button at the bottom of the page to create your dataset version. Step 5: Train a Bottle Cap Inspection Model With a dataset ready, you can train a model to inspect bottle caps. To start training a model, click the "Train Model" button on your dataset page. A pop up will appear in which you can configure your model training job. From this pop up, select “ RF-DETR small ” architecture. Once you have configured your training job, an estimate will appear that shows roughly how long it should take to train your model. You can monitor your training job in real time from your dataset page. Once your training job has been allocated to a machine, a graph will appear that shows the performance of your model as it trains. You will receive an email once your model has trained. When your model has finished training, you can test it from the "Test" tab available in the sidebar of your project. Here is an example of our model running to identify a no cap: Our model successfully identified that a bottle cap isn't visible. Step 6: Create a Workflow In order to automate this task of inspecting bottle caps, assemble a custom workflow using Roboflow Workflows : Create a workflow by going to the "Workflows" tab on the left and clicking "Create Workflow": Add an Object Detection Model block. Set the block name to model and set the model ID to your model ID (ex. bottle-cap-integrity-gb3ey/2). This block processes your input image and outputs bounding box coordinates with class predictions. Add a Bounding Box Visualization block below the model node. Connect the workflow input image and model.predictions into it. This step renders detection boxes on the original image frame. Add a Label Visualization block below the bounding box node. Pass the image output from bounding_box_visualization into this block to overlay class names and confidence scores on top of the boxes. Finally, specify the workflows outputs: Step 7: Deploy the Bottle Cap Inspection Model With a workflow ready, you can deploy it on your own hardware using Roboflow Inference . Roboflow Inference is high-performance software that lets you run computer vision models on images, videos, live camera streams, and RTSP streams. For this guide, we will test our model on an image. Refer to the Inference documentation to learn how to deploy a model on a camera stream in real time. To get started, we need to install Inference. We also need to install supervision , a Python package with utilities for working with computer vision models. To install the required dependencies, run the following command: pip install --user inference-sdk python-dotenv Next, you need to export your Roboflow API key into your environment. To do so, set an environment variable called RF_API_KEY : RF_API_KEY="insert_your_api_key_here" Learn how to retrieve your Roboflow API key. Next, create a Python file and add the following code: # 1. Import the library from inference_sdk import InferenceHTTPClient import os import base64 from dotenv import load_dotenv load_dotenv() IMAGE_PATH = "bottle.png" # 2. Connect to your workflow client = InferenceHTTPClient( api_url="https://serverless.roboflow.com", api_key=os.environ.get("RF_API_KEY") ) # 3. Run your workflow on an image result = client.run_workflow( workspace_name="aarnavs-space", workflow_id="bottle-cap-annotated", images={ "image": IMAGE_PATH # Path to your image file }, use_cache=False # The cache can serve a stale workflow after edits; set True once the workflow is stable ) # 4. Get your results predictions = result[0]["predictions"]["predictions"] print(predictions) # 5. The workflow draws the boxes in the cloud so you can just save the returned image with open("annotated.png", "wb") as f: f.write(base64.b64decode(result[0]["annotated_image"])) print("Saved annotated.png") Above, replace bottle-cap-annotated with your workflow ID. Replace bottle.png with the name of the image on which you want to run inference. Let’s run the code on an image where a bottle cap isn't visible. Here are the results: Our model successfully identified that the bottle cap wasn't there. You can integrate this system into your business logic. For example, you can automatically reject bottles whose caps are not properly sealed. You can count the number of bottles whose caps were not properly sealed or were missing each day to monitor defect rates over time. Bottle Cap Inspection with AI In this guide, we built a bottle cap inspection system with computer vision. Our system was trained to identify properly sealed bottle caps, bottle caps that are not properly sealed, and bottles that are missing caps. To do this, we gathered images showing these bottle cap statuses, labeled them, then trained a vision model. We then deployed our system onto our own hardware using Roboflow Inference . title: The New Economics of Brand Integrity: What the Data Says in 2026
summary: New data from MarqVision’s 2026 State of Brand Integrity Report reveals how AI-driven counterfeits and impersonation are reshaping brand protection. Discover the revenue impact, why takedown metrics are failing, and how leading brands are shifting to outcome-based measurement.
body_text: Brand protection is no longer a background operational function. In 2026, it has become a measurable economic lever: one that directly impacts revenue, demand stability, and brand trust. ‍ New data from MarqVision’s 2026 State of Brand Integrity Report , based on insights from 96 brand leaders, shows an industry at a clear inflection point. While threats have accelerated dramatically, the way brands measure and manage protection is starting to change. ‍ AI Has Changed the Cost Structure Of Growth One of the most striking findings from the research is how widespread AI-enabled threats have become. ‍ 85% of brands report experiencing AI-accelerated threats, including fake listings, impersonation accounts, and synthetic brand assets 82% say counterfeit and impersonation issues are worse than two years ago Generative AI has lowered the barrier to imitation. High-fidelity replicas of products, storefronts, domains, and marketing assets can now be created on-demand, often surfacing within days, or even hours, of a legitimate campaign or viral moment. ‍ The result is what many brand leaders now recognize as an “AI tax” on growth: marketing still drives demand, but a portion of that demand is silently diverted before it reaches authorized channels. ‍ Viral Moments Now Trigger Instant Exploitation Speed is now one of the defining risk factors. ‍ According to the data: ‍ 57% of brands see fake accounts or websites appear within one week of a viral moment 24% see impersonation within just 24–48 hours ‍ Impersonation often arrives first, because it requires no physical production, only a domain or social account. Counterfeits follow shortly after, extracting even more value. ‍ This matters because the financial impact is no longer marginal: in fact, 78% of brands estimate losing 5% or more of annual revenue to counterfeits and impersonation combined Why Takedown Metrics Are Breaking Down Despite rising losses, many organizations are still measuring brand protection by activity rather than impact. ‍ 50% still prioritize takedown counts as their primary metric Only 35% actively track revenue recovered or protected This creates a paradox: higher takedown volume often signals a larger underlying problem, not progress. Faster removals don’t necessarily mean cleaner search results, safer customers, or stabilized demand. ‍ An Industry at an Inflection Point The research reveals a clean divide in how brands define success. ‍ 50% prioritize revenue protected 50% still prioritize total takedowns executed 85% agree brand protection should shift to revenue and business outcomes This gap between where brands want to go and where they actually are represents both risk and opportunity. Brands that make the shift first gain clearer visibility into exposure, stronger executive alignment, and a more defensible case for investment. ‍ The Full Picture These insights are just a snapshot. ‍ Our 2026 Brand Integrity Report goes deeper into: ‍ How leading brands are quantifying revenue loss and recovery ‍ The metrics replacing takedown volume ‍ What differentiates teams that have transformed enforcement from those still stuck in reactive mode ‍ Where brand protection is heading as AI-driven discovery becomes mainstream Want to learn more? Check out the full Brand Integrity Report here.

title: KIMBERLY-CLARK UNVEILS PROPRIETARY ALTERNATIVE NATURAL FIBER INNOVATION PROGRAM TO ADVANCE ITS "BETTER CARE FOR A BETTER WORLD" COMMITMENT
summary: The Investor Relations website contains information about Kimberly-Clark Corporation's business for stockholders, potential investors, and financial analysts.
body_text: Release Details KIMBERLY-CLARK UNVEILS PROPRIETARY ALTERNATIVE NATURAL FIBER INNOVATION PROGRAM TO ADVANCE ITS "BETTER CARE FOR A BETTER WORLD" COMMITMENT Aug 3, 2026 PDF Version Company Pioneers Next-Generation, Agriculture-Based Materials Platform to Reshape How It Manufactures Hygiene Products DALLAS , Aug. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Kimberly-Clark Corporation (NASDAQ: KMB) today unveiled a proprietary innovation program focused on advancing alternative natural fibers as the foundation for a next-generation, high-performance, sustainable materials platform, furthering the Company's commitment to Better Care for a Better World. Company researchers and scientists developed a patented technology platform by transforming fibers from a rapidly renewable succulent plant into sustainable material. This breakthrough has the potential to power the Company's future hygiene products with enhanced performance, quality, and sustainability.* "This represents an exciting moonshot for Kimberly-Clark and the culmination of more than two decades of materials and plant science expertise," said Craig Slavtcheff, Chief Research and Development Officer at Kimberly-Clark. "We have developed a highly proprietary technology platform rooted in alternative fiber research and believe that these novel natural fibers will form our next great materials platform – an innovation with the potential to reshape the hygiene category. While testing continues, we are optimistic by early results and believe this material will provide curve-bending performance in our products while strengthening our long-term growth and supply chain resilience and accelerating our journey toward a future less dependent on traditional fiber sources." The Alternative Natural Fiber program reflects Kimberly-Clark's consumer-led innovation platform model, which focuses on making strategic investments in disruptive technologies. This approach aims to deliver the best product at the lowest cost, while upholding responsible stewardship of the resources essential to the Company's offerings. Kimberly-Clark expects products developed with this alternative fiber to support its strategy of focusing on higher-value, differentiated spaces where it has the right to win. "Kimberly-Clark is at its best when we harness the power of science to solve real human needs and deliver Better Care for a Better World ," said Jeff Melucci, Chief Strategy, Business Development, and Administrative Officer at Kimberly-Clark. "Our Alternative Natural Fiber program is an example of our Powering Care strategy in motion and how we are pushing the boundaries of what we can deliver to consumers to meaningfully enhance how they experience products they rely on every day. We are energized by all the ways this promising innovation can reset the standards in our product categories, while delivering the care consumers seek from us and ongoing value to our shareholders." ABOUT THE ALTERNATIVE NATURAL FIBER INNOVATION PROGRAM After evaluating more than 70 fiber candidates across performance, sustainability and cost criteria, Kimberly-Clark research scientists identified a promising solution in hesperaloe, a native, low-water-use plant that thrives in the arid climate of the Southwest United States. The Company's innovation program, based in Yuma, Arizona, has demonstrated this plant and its proprietary technologies yield a rapidly renewable natural fiber source that carries the performance and quality standards consumers expect from Kimberly-Clark's trusted brands. As part of this innovation program, Kimberly-Clark is building a pilot facility in Yuma and hiring local, specialized talent to support it. The Company is also collaborating with growers, technical experts, and community stakeholders in Arizona, California, and across the broader U.S. Southwest to evaluate hesperaloe's potential as a year-round source of agricultural and economic opportunity. Compared with several crops currently grown in the region, hesperaloe requires less water to cultivate, offering potential benefits for growers, local communities, and regional water stewardship efforts. Kimberly-Clark believes its Alternative Natural Fiber has the potential to be integrated across its hygiene products portfolio, accelerating its efforts to deliver consumer-inspired, science-driven innovation, strengthening its long-term fiber supply resilience, and advancing responsible stewardship of natural resources. *Based on internal Kimberly-Clark research and development testing of Alternative Natural Fibers compared with traditional forest-based fibers used in the Company's current hygiene products. About Kimberly-Clark Kimberly-Clark (NASDAQ: KMB) and its trusted brands are an indispensable part of life for people in more than 175 countries and territories. Our portfolio of brands, including Huggies, Kleenex, Scott, Kotex, Cottonelle, Poise, Depend, Pull-Ups, Goodnites, Intimus, Plenitud, Sweety, Softex, Viva and WypAll, hold No. 1 or No. 2 share positions in approximately 70 countries. Our company's purpose is to deliver Better Care for a Better World. We are committed to using sustainable practices designed to support a healthy planet, build strong communities, and enable our business to thrive for decades to come. To keep up with the latest news and learn more about the company's more than 150-year history of innovation, visit the Kimberly-Clark website. title: CAC 40 ETF: comparison and how they work (2026)
summary: CAC 40 ETFs track France's flagship Paris stock exchange index. How they work, their PEA eligibility and the most widely used funds in 2026.
body_text: Updated on 7 August 2026 A CAC 40 ETF is an exchange-traded fund that replicates the performance of the 40 largest companies listed on the Paris stock exchange, with very low management fees. This article compares the main CAC 40 ETFs, their eligibility for the PEA (a French tax-advantaged equity savings account) and their advantages and drawbacks. Key takeaways The most widely used CAC 40 ETFs are Amundi's, with direct physical replication and a Total Expense Ratio (TER) of 0.25%. Most CAC 40 ETFs are eligible for the PEA, combining exposure to the French market with the tax advantages of that wrapper. The CAC 40 is a price index that excludes the dividends paid out, unlike the CAC 40 GR, which reinvests them. The main risk of CAC 40 ETFs is concentration: performance depends heavily on the largest constituents of the index. CAC 40: general information Sector composition The CAC 40 index comprises the 40 largest companies listed on the Paris stock exchange , selected on their market capitalisation and their liquidity . These companies span a wide range of sectors of the French economy, from healthcare to carmaking, taking in finance, energy and telecoms, among many others. The index includes French giants such as L'Oréal, Sanofi and Renault. This sector spread gives investors balanced exposure to the various segments of the French economy, easing the diversification of their portfolios . Historical performance The CAC 40 is seen as a barometer of the French economy and gives an indication of the overall performance of the French stock market . Moves in the index can be driven by a variety of factors, including companies' financial results , political decisions, global economic events and market trends . Since it was created in 1987, the index has posted an average annual return of around 5.5% to 6% excluding dividends, based on a level close to 8,700 points in early August 2026 ( Euronext ). Past performance is not a reliable indicator of future performance. That growth may look modest next to other international stock market indices. It is worth noting, however, that the CAC 40 does not include the dividends distributed by its constituent companies. An index that leaves dividends out The CAC 40 is a price index , which means it does not account for the dividends paid by its constituent companies. The performance of the index therefore does not necessarily reflect the full returns an investor could achieve by investing in those companies. An investor holding an ETF tracking the CAC 40, for instance, would earn returns from share price movements, but not necessarily from the dividends those companies pay. To gauge its true performance, look at the CAC 40 GR , which stands for Gross Return and reinvests dividends. According to Euronext, the operator of the Paris stock exchange, the CAC 40 GR stood at 27,721 points on 14 July 2026, an annualised return of around 8.9% since the index was created in 1987. Past performance is not a reliable indicator of future performance. The chart above shows how the two indices have diverged since 2009. Centralise your wealth PEA, savings accounts, cryptocurrencies, stocks, real estate, bank accounts. Discover Finary Why invest in a CAC 40 ETF? Investing in a CAC 40 ETF gives diversified exposure to the 40 largest French companies in a single trade, simply and at low cost. The main reasons to consider one: Diversification : A CAC 40 ETF gives investors diversified exposure to the 40 largest listed French companies. That reduces the risk attached to holding individual shares, because the portfolio's performance is tied to the CAC 40 index as a whole. Simplicity : ETFs are as easy to buy and sell as shares. Unlike managing a portfolio of individual stocks, investors do not have to pick and monitor each company. The CAC 40 ETF already handles that selection for you. Large-cap exposure : The companies in the CAC 40 are among the largest listed capitalisations in France. A CAC 40 ETF provides exposure to their share price performance, with no guarantee of returns. On top of these benefits, a CAC 40 ETF also offers high liquidity . Because ETFs trade on an exchange, units can be bought or sold at any time during market hours. Investors can therefore react quickly to market moves and manage their portfolio flexibly. Good to know : In short, a CAC 40 ETF lets investors diversify their portfolio, gain exposure to the performance of large French companies and benefit from high liquidity and low fees . It is one way of gaining exposure to the French stock market. Whether a given product suits you depends on your personal situation. Examples of CAC 40 ETFs Here are some examples of CAC 40 ETFs available on the market: ETF ISIN Management fees Domicile Distribution type Assets under management Amundi CAC 40 ESG UCITS ETF Dist LU1681047079 0.25% Luxembourg Dividends distributed €42 million Amundi CAC 40 ESG UCITS ETF Acc LU1681046931 0.25% Luxembourg Dividends reinvested €785 million Amundi CAC 40 UCITS ETF Acc FR0013380607 0.25% France Dividends reinvested €1.096 billion These three ETFs are among the most widely used on the market. They all track the CAC 40 index (or its CAC 40 ESG variant), but differ in their distribution policy: some pay dividends out to investors (Dist), others reinvest them automatically in the fund (Acc). Can you hold a CAC 40 ETF in a PEA? Yes. You can invest in a CAC 40 ETF through a PEA (Plan d'Épargne en Actions) , provided the ETF is domiciled in the European Union and tracks a European equity index. In return, the PEA offers tax advantages on investments in French and European shares. Here is the list of eligible CAC 40 ETFs: Amundi CAC 40 ESG UCITS ETF Dist (ISIN: LU1681047079) Amundi CAC 40 ESG UCITS ETF Acc (ISIN: LU1681046931) Amundi CAC 40 UCITS ETF Acc (ISIN: FR0013380607) Amundi CAC 40 Daily (2x) Leveraged UCITS ETF Acc (ISIN: FR0010592014) - leveraged product, higher risk Amundi ETF Short CAC 40 Daily UCITS ETF (ISIN: FR0010717124) - inverse product, higher risk, for experienced investors only BNP Paribas Easy CAC 40 ESG UCITS ETF (ISIN: FR0010150458) Good to know : These ETFs are all PEA-eligible, with management fees of 0.25% a year for the standard versions and higher (0.35% to 0.40%) for the leveraged or inverse versions. Investors can therefore combine exposure to CAC 40 companies with the tax advantages of the PEA. These products can be considered within a PEA, subject to your own analysis of your tax situation. Advantages of CAC 40 ETFs CAC 40 ETFs offer investors several advantages: Diversified exposure : CAC 40 ETFs give investors diversified exposure to the largest listed French companies. Liquidity : CAC 40 ETFs are generally liquid, meaning investors can buy and sell units easily on the market. Tools such as Finary also centralise the tracking of ETF, stock and other asset positions across every broker. Fees : ETFs generally carry lower management fees than traditional mutual funds, which can work in investors' favour. Drawbacks of CAC 40 ETFs There are also a few drawbacks to bear in mind: Market risk : Like any stock market investment, CAC 40 ETFs are exposed to market risk. The value of units can fluctuate with the CAC 40 index. Concentration risk : Because the CAC 40 ETF is weighted by market capitalisation, it is heavily influenced by the performance of the largest CAC 40 companies. That creates a concentration risk if some of those companies run into financial difficulty. Several ETF options are available, each with advantages and drawbacks to weigh. It is also possible to hold a CAC 40 ETF inside a PEA, adding tax advantages. Before investing, do your own research, consider speaking to a financial adviser and make sure you understand the risks attached to any investment. CAC 40 ETFs can be a useful tool for investors who want exposure to economic growth in France and want to diversify their portfolio. Frequently asked questions Which CAC 40 ETFs are most often mentioned? The right choice depends on each investor's situation and objectives. CAC 40 ETFs can be bought through a brokerage platform or a bank offering brokerage services. Search for the ETF's ticker and place a buy order. What is the difference between the CAC 40 and the CAC 40 GR? The CAC 40 is a price index that does not account for the dividends paid by its constituent companies. The CAC 40 GR (Gross Return) reinvests those dividends and therefore reflects the actual return an investor obtains over the long term. Is a CAC 40 ETF risky? Like any equity investment, a CAC 40 ETF carries a risk of capital loss and a concentration risk, because its performance depends heavily on the largest companies in the index. It is therefore not suited to a very short investment horizon. title: Best HubSpot Alternatives 2026: Platforms for Every CRM Need
summary: Discover the best HubSpot alternatives in 2026: honest comparison of cost, features, and flexibility for CRM buyers seeking a better fit.
body_text: TL;DR: For teams seeking a HubSpot alternative, Salesforce, ActiveCampaign, Pipedrive, Zoho, EngageBay, Freshworks, Mailchimp, and Miniloop each win on different priorities. Miniloop stands out for businesses demanding custom CRM workflows and sizable cost reductions by eliminating per-seat fees. Best HubSpot Alternatives 2026: Platforms for Every CRM Need Last updated: August 2026 The top hubspot alternatives are Miniloop (most customizable & cost-saving, No per-seat fees; annual cost covers initial build, support, and updates.), Salesforce (most scalable & feature-rich), ActiveCampaign (best for SMB email & automation), Pipedrive (best for pipeline sales teams), Zoho (most comprehensive business suite), EngageBay (best value all-in-one for small business), Freshworks (best for support-driven CRM), Mailchimp (quickest email-first CRM option). HubSpot remains one of the most recognized CRM and marketing platforms, but 2026 brings sharper scrutiny of high subscription costs and the inflexibility of generic business workflows. With more organizations needing tailored CRM stacks and holding tighter to their data, the appetite for alternatives, especially those that cut recurring SaaS costs or offer infrastructure independence, has never been higher. Meanwhile, new options and custom builds are filling gaps traditional platforms miss. Why people look for HubSpot alternatives Teams outgrowing HubSpot often hit the same ceiling: rising subscription costs (especially per-seat fees), restrictive workflow options, and difficulty aligning the platform to unique business processes. body_text: Today, we launched Bujeti Smart Payment Links, the fastest way to request and receive payments directly from your Bujeti dashboard. For most Nigerian businesses, getting paid is rarely where the story ends. The moment the money lands, the real work begins. The default workflow looks like this: Share account details Wait for the transfer Ask for proof of payment Search through bank notifications Confirm manually Notify the customer Categorise the transaction by hand Update budgets and internal records Reconcile it against the right invoice, and again at month end Each step is a place where information gets lost, delayed, or duplicated. The combined cost is real: delayed cash flow, hours swallowed by reconciliation, avoidable payment errors, and no reliable visibility into what is pending versus paid, let alone what has actually been recognised as revenue. Collecting business payments just got smarter Since we launched Bujeti, our vision has been consistent: to build the Finance Control Centre for African businesses. We started by helping companies gain better control over money leaving the business through budgets, approval workflows, corporate cards, expense management, and spend controls. Those tools solved one side of the financial equation by giving finance teams greater visibility into how money was being spent and ensuring every expense followed the right approval process. But finance doesn't stop at spend. A finance platform that only manages spend is only telling half the story. To truly understand cash flow, finance teams need a connected view of collections, invoices, payments, and reconciliation alongside their budgets and expenses. That's why we've continued expanding Bujeti beyond spend management. First came Invoicing, making it easier to bill customers professionally. Then Virtual Accounts and Bank Connect, helping businesses monitor incoming funds with greater visibility. Today, we're adding another important piece to that ecosystem with Smart Payment Links. Smart Payment Links is part of a broader vision to bring every financial workflow into one connected platform, where requesting payment, receiving funds, tracking collections, and reconciling transactions happen from the same dashboard your team already uses every day. Meet Bujeti Smart Payment Links Bujeti Smart Payment Links gives businesses a faster and more professional way to collect payments. Every payment is automatically categorised, budgeted, tagged, recognised as revenue, reconciled, synced to your accounting software, and even split across partners when needed. Instead of copying account details into WhatsApp, email, or social media conversations, you simply generate a secure payment page and share a single link. Your customer opens the link, reviews the payment information, and completes the transaction through a branded checkout experience using their preferred payment method, whether that's card, bank transfer, or USSD. That means up to 70% less admin, fewer manual tasks, and more time to focus on serving customers, growing revenue, and running your business. The work that happens after the money lands Most payment tools stop the moment a transaction clears. Ours keeps going. The moment payment is completed, Bujeti updates the payment status automatically and notifies your team, categorises the transaction, applies it to the right budget, tags it as revenue, and syncs it to your accounting software, automatically. If you split revenue with a partner, it splits it. If it is a recurring payment, it repeats on schedule. Nobody touches a spreadsheet, and nobody waits until month-end to know what actually came in. Because Payment Links is built directly into Bujeti, collections don't exist in isolation. They become part of the same financial workflow that already includes invoices, approvals, budgets, reporting, and spend management. That means your finance team isn't jumping between different systems to understand what's been paid, what's still outstanding, and how collections affect the wider financial picture. Creating a Smart Payment Link takes less than a minute We wanted the process to feel as simple as sending a message. Creating a Payment Link takes less than a minute: Navigate to Links from your Bujeti dashboard. Click Create Payment Link . Enter the payment amount and transaction details. Generate your secure payment link. Share it through whichever channel you're already using to communicate with your customer. If you also need to issue an invoice, you don't have to start the process again. Using the same payment information, Bujeti can generate an invoice without requiring duplicate data entry, helping your team move faster while keeping records accurate and consistent. What changes for your business Everything lives in one place: Your collections sit alongside your budgets, invoices, and spend, not in a separate tool your finance team has to check on the side. Your books stay current on their own: Every payment is categorised, budgeted, and synced to your accounting software automatically, so your numbers reflect reality in real time, not at month end. Revenue sharing takes care of itself: If you split income with a partner, the link divides it for you, every time, without anyone doing the maths by hand. Your team stops chasing: Following up on payment status, proof, and reconciliation is administrative work dressed up as account management. Smart Link removes most of it. You still make the right impression at the point of payment: A branded checkout carries more weight than an account number in a chat, whether you are collecting ₦50,000 or ₦50 million. Built for businesses that collect payments every day Nearly every business will feel this, but a few will feel it immediately because collecting payment is such a constant part of how they operate. SaaS and software companies bill subscriptions, onboarding fees, and renewals on a repeating cycle. Recurring payments and automatic syncing to accounting software mean revenue is booked and recognised without finance re-entering it every month. In travel and hospitality, a high volume of bookings across multiple properties makes categorisation and reconciliation constant work. Smart Link handles both automatically, so finance sees accurate, real-time revenue by property without closing books by hand. For real estate businesses, inspection fees, reservation deposits, and installment span months. Automatic budgeting and revenue tagging keep every project's cash position current without someone manually tracking which payment belongs to which unit. Professional service firms invoice frequently and often split fees with partners or associates. Automatic revenue sharing means everyone gets their share the moment a client pays, with no manual splitting after the fact. E-commerce businesses sell across social media, messaging apps, and marketplaces, and need every sale accounted for the same way regardless of channel. Smart Link categorises and reconciles every payment identically, wherever it came from. Although these industries feel it first, the underlying idea holds for any business that collects payments repeatedly: it is worth having those payments do the accounting work themselves. It's live now Bujeti Smart Payment Links is available on your Bujeti dashboard today. Log in , create your first link, and share it with your next customer. It is one more piece of a single, connected platform, where the money coming in works exactly as hard as the money going out, and everything closes itself out in the same place, seen by the same team, in real time.

title: Why 74% of Real Estate Leads Go to the First Agent Who Responds
summary: The National Association of Realtors has a stat that should terrify every real estate team: 74% of buyers work with the first agent who gives them useful
body_text: The National Association of Realtors has a stat that should terrify every real estate team: 74% of buyers work with the first agent who gives them useful information. Not the best agent. Not the most experienced agent. The first one. If your average lead response time is 2–8 hours (which is the industry average for most brokerages), you're losing the race before it starts. The team down the street that responds in 3 minutes is getting the showing — and eventually the commission — on leads you paid to generate. Here's what the fastest teams are doing differently. The real estate speed problem Real estate leads come from everywhere: Zillow, Realtor.com, Google Ads, Facebook, open houses, yard signs, referrals, and the brokerage website. Each source has different lead quality, different intent levels, and different expectations for response speed. The standard process at most brokerages: lead comes in → lands in the CRM → gets round-robined to the next agent → agent gets an email notification → agent checks email whenever they check email → agent calls (if they feel like it). Average time from lead submission to first agent contact: 2–8 hours. For leads that come in after business hours or on weekends: 12–24 hours. In those 2–24 hours, the buyer has already submitted inquiries to 2–3 other agents or teams. The first one to respond with something useful (not a generic "thanks for your interest" autoresponder) wins the conversation. What "useful information" means The NAR stat specifies "useful information" — not just speed. A generic auto-reply doesn't count. A personalized response that demonstrates you understand what the buyer is looking for does. Response type Speed Usefulness Result Generic autoresponder ("Thanks for your inquiry, an agent will be in touch") Instant Zero — tells the buyer nothing useful Buyer keeps searching. Doesn't feel engaged. Agent calls back manually 2–8 hours High when it happens — real conversation Too late. Buyer already engaged with a faster responder. Personalized auto-response ("Hi Sarah, I see you're interested in 3-bedroom homes in Brookline under $600K. I've connected you with Mike, our Brookline specialist. Here's his calendar.") Under 3 minutes High — shows you read their request, matched them to a relevant agent, and gave them a clear next step Buyer feels understood. Books with Mike. The third option wins because it's both fast AND useful. It requires knowing what the buyer is looking for (captured on the form), who the right agent is (routing logic), and how to reach them (scheduling link). That's infrastructure, not hustle. How the fastest teams are structured The teams consistently responding in under 3 minutes share four characteristics: They qualify on the form. The form asks: buying or selling? Budget range? Timeline? Pre-approved? Neighborhood preferences? This takes 60 seconds for the buyer to complete and gives the system everything it needs to route and respond intelligently. They route by specialization, not rotation. A buyer looking for a $2M home in a luxury neighborhood goes to the luxury specialist who knows that market. A first-time buyer looking at condos under $400K goes to an agent who specializes in first-time buyers. Round-robin would send both to whoever's next in line — regardless of fit. They auto-respond with specificity. The instant response references the buyer's criteria, names the matched agent, and includes a scheduling link. It's personalized enough to feel human and fast enough to beat every competitor. They tier by intent. Pre-approved buyers with a 0–90 day timeline get the premium treatment: instant response, agent call within 10 minutes, curated listing package. Casual browsers 12+ months out get an automated nurture — monthly market updates and neighborhood guides — with no agent time invested. The math for a 25-agent brokerage Metric Current (2–8 hr response) Optimized (< 3 min response) Monthly leads from all sources 400 400 Lead-to-showing rate 10% 30% Showings per month 40 120 Average conversion (showing to offer) 20% 20% Offers per month 8 24 Average commission $12,000 $12,000 Monthly commission revenue $96,000 $288,000 Same leads. Same agents. 3x the revenue. The difference is the infrastructure between lead submission and agent contact. Where Surface fits Surface handles the full flow: qualification forms that capture buyer/seller intent, attribute-based routing to the right agent by geography and specialization, instant personalized response within seconds, and tiered follow-up based on intent level. All connected to your CRM (Follow Up Boss, kvCORE, HubSpot). If your team's lead-to-showing rate is below 15%, the problem isn't lead quality. It's response speed and routing accuracy. Surface was built to fix both.

title: FDA Announces Massive Recall of Rohto Eye Drops Over Sterility Concerns: What Consumers Need to Know

body_text: More Than 11 Million Eye Drop Packages Recalled Across the United States Millions of consumers across the United States are being urged to check their medicine cabinets after a major recall involving Rohto Cooling Eye Drops. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has announced that more than 11 million packages of several Rohto eye drop products are being recalled because of concerns related to product sterility. Eye drops are designed to come into direct contact with one of the body's most sensitive organs. Because of this, any potential contamination or manufacturing issue can increase the risk of eye irritation, infection, or other health complications. While the FDA has not reported confirmed injuries linked to this recall, the agency has classified the action as a Class II recall, indicating that temporary or medically reversible health effects are possible. This article explains why the recall was issued, which products are affected, what consumers should do next, and why sterility is essential for eye care products. Why Are the Rohto Eye Drops Being Recalled? According to the FDA enforcement report, Vietnam-based Rohto-Mentholatum Co., Ltd. voluntarily initiated the recall after identifying a lack of assurance of sterility in certain eye drop products. Sterility is one of the most important quality standards for ophthalmic medications. Since eye drops are applied directly into the eyes, they must remain completely free of harmful microorganisms or contaminants during manufacturing and packaging. Although the FDA did not release additional technical details regarding the manufacturing issue, the concern was significant enough for multiple product lots to be recalled nationwide. The recall began on July 14, 2026, and the FDA officially classified it on July 23, 2026. What Does a Class II Recall Mean? The FDA uses different classifications to communicate the level of health risk associated with recalled products. A Class II recall means that using the affected product may cause temporary or medically reversible health problems. The likelihood of severe or life-threatening consequences is considered low, but consumers are still advised not to use the recalled products. While this category is less serious than a Class I recall, it should not be ignored, particularly when the products are intended for eye care. Which Rohto Eye Drops Are Included? The recall affects several popular Rohto Cooling Eye Drops sold throughout the United States. The impacted products include: Rohto Cooling Eye Drops All-In-One Rohto Cooling Eye Drops Max Strength Rohto Cooling Eye Drops Optic Glow Rohto Cooling Eye Drops Digi Eye Rohto Cooling Eye Drops Dry Aid Rohto Cooling Eye Drops Cool Relief According to the FDA, the recall covers approximately 11.96 million cartons containing more than 12.46 million bottles. Consumers should carefully inspect product packaging and expiration dates before using any Rohto Cooling Eye Drops. The affected products have expiration dates ranging from July 2026 through February 2029. Why Sterility Matters in Eye Drops Unlike many over-the-counter medications, eye drops bypass many of the body's natural protective barriers. Even tiny amounts of bacteria, fungi, or other contaminants can potentially lead to: Eye irritation Redness Pain Blurred vision Eye infections Corneal damage in severe cases Maintaining sterility throughout the manufacturing process helps ensure that products remain safe until they reach consumers. If sterility cannot be guaranteed, manufacturers often issue recalls as a precaution to reduce potential health risks. Previous Eye Drop Safety Concerns This is not the first major eye drop recall in recent years. In 2023, the FDA warned consumers to stop using more than two dozen over-the-counter eye drop products sold under several retail brands after concerns that contamination could lead to serious eye infections and possible vision loss. That same year, health officials investigated an outbreak involving drug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteria linked to contaminated artificial tears and eye drops. The outbreak resulted in severe infections and highlighted the importance of strict manufacturing standards for ophthalmic products. These incidents have increased public awareness regarding eye drop safety and manufacturing quality control. What Should Consumers Do? If you currently own any Rohto Cooling Eye Drops, take the following precautions: Check the product name and expiration date. Compare your product with the FDA recall notice. Stop using any affected product immediately. Contact the retailer or manufacturer regarding return or refund instructions. Speak with your healthcare provider if you experience eye pain, redness, swelling, unusual discharge, blurred vision, or other concerning symptoms after using the product. Consumers should never continue using a recalled eye care product, even if it appears unopened or unused. Are All Rohto Products Affected? No. The recall only applies to specific lots of selected Rohto Cooling Eye Drops listed in the FDA enforcement report. Other Rohto products that are not included in the recall are not affected based on the current FDA announcement. Consumers should verify lot information using official FDA recall notices or contact the manufacturer if they are uncertain. FDA Continues Monitoring Product Safety The FDA routinely oversees recalls involving medications, medical devices, and consumer health products to help protect public health. Manufacturers may voluntarily recall products when quality issues are discovered during internal testing or inspections. The FDA then evaluates the situation and assigns an appropriate recall classification based on the potential health risks. Although no widespread injuries have been publicly linked to this Rohto recall, consumers are encouraged to remain informed and follow official guidance. Final Thoughts The recall of more than 11 million packages of Rohto Cooling Eye Drops serves as a reminder of the importance of manufacturing quality and product safety in healthcare products. While the FDA has categorized the recall as presenting a relatively low risk of serious harm, eye health should never be taken lightly. Consumers should review their eye care products, discontinue use of any recalled items, and consult a healthcare professional if they notice unusual symptoms after using the affected products. Staying informed about FDA recalls can help reduce unnecessary health risks and ensure that the products you use meet established safety standards. Source The Epoch Times and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) recall enforcement report. Disclaimer This article is intended for informational and educational purposes only and should not be considered medical advice. Readers should refer to official FDA announcements and consult a qualified healthcare professional regarding any medical concerns or questions about recalled products.

title: Red, White, and Blue-Chip: 7 Significant American Cars Selling in Monterey
summary: Every year, the Monterey auctions assemble the most expensive consignment lists of any public sale anywhere in the world. Many of these princely automobiles date from the 1930s, 1950s, and 1960s, and many of them are from the other side of the Atlantic. Of the 10 most expensive cars ever sold at the Monterey auctions, […]
body_text: Every year, the Monterey auctions assemble the most expensive consignment lists of any public sale anywhere in the world. Many of these princely automobiles date from the 1930s, 1950s, and 1960s, and many of them are from the other side of the Atlantic. Of the 10 most expensive cars ever sold at the Monterey auctions, almost all of them are either Italian or English. Just one hails from the U.S. of A. In 2026, though, we can’t help but notice that there are some serious heavy hitters from our shores that are crossing the block. Historically significant, interesting, rare stuff: Duesenbergs, Cobras, L88s, V-12 Packards, etc. Below are our favorites. 1968 Chevrolet Corvette L88 RED/NART Le Mans RM Sotheby's RM Sotheby’s, Lot 350 Corvettes have a long history of racing in Europe, and even though success was mixed in the early years, this car was one of the highlights. Its story starts with a Florida team called Race Engineering & Development (RED), which had great success in U.S. sports car racing with an L88-powered 1969 model, painted in Confederate flag livery and dubbed the “Rebel Corvette.” The RED team soon set their sights on Le Mans, but the French officials rejected their application. Undeterred, they were able to get a hold of Luigi Chinetti, owner of the North American Racing Team (NART). A Le Mans veteran and winner, Chinetti happened to have four entries for the 1972 Le Mans race, and he agreed to give the Corvette boys his reserve spot, on the condition that their Chevrolet wear the same livery as Chinetti’s Ferraris. The RED team built up a new car for the race, sourcing a wrecked ’68 Corvette and installing L88 components. Le Mans would be the car’s very first race, and in practice it sustained front-end damage. The team repaired it with a combination of aluminum, pieces of a wooden shipping crate, and duct tape. It started the race in 51st place, fifth from last, and there were fuel issues as well as significant rain, but drivers Dave Heinz and Bob Johnson made it up to 15th place overall and first in class by the checkered flag, becoming only the fourth Corvette up to that point to finish the 24-hour test of endurance. After returning to the U.S., the car got its own Confederate flag livery and was campaigned with the original Rebel Corvette in the 1972 season. In 1973, it finished third at the 24 Hours of Daytona behind a 911 Carrera RSR and Ferrari 365 GTB/4. It ran as high as second overall at Sebring but retired, and continued to race in 1973 and ’74. It was restored in the ’90s back to its original Le Mans appearance, and has a $900,000–$1,100,000 estimate for Monterey. 1913 Mercer Model 35-J Raceabout Darin Schnabel/RM Sotheby's Darin Schnabel/RM Sotheby's RM Sotheby’s, Lot 127 In 1913, the Corvette wouldn’t come out for another 40 years. America already had a sports car, though, and that was the Mercer Raceabout. Founded in 1909 in Trenton, New Jersey (which is in Mercer County), the Mercer Automobile Company was led by the Roebling family (of Brooklyn Bridge fame) and completed its first cars in 1910. The Raceabout is Mercer’s most famous creation. At 4.9 liters, its T-head four-cylinder was actually somewhat small compared to other performance cars of the day, but it made a respectable 55 horsepower and the roadster it powered didn’t weigh much at all, thanks to that rollerskate of a body and low-slung chassis. Each Raceabout came with a guarantee of 70 mph, and modified cars could hit 100. Most cars on the road back then struggled to go 45. With a price tag of about 2500 bucks back when median household income was roughly 700, the Raceabout’s target audience was wealthy sportsmen, and many of them went racing. The one on offer in Monterey is a 1913 model, and thus comes with the sought-after four-speed (up from three). According to RM Sotheby’s, its known history goes back to 1939, when a collector found it in a storage garage and paid just $62.50 for it. In 2026, however, you’ll need $2.75M to $3.5M, according to the presale estimate. 1966 Shelby 427 Cobra Roadster Mecum Mecum, Lot S96 A fat-fendered 427 car, in blue with white Le Mans stripes, is the quintessential Cobra. It’s the look that so many of the kit cars and diecast models ape, but this one is the real deal, and it has led quite a life. It reportedly went to New York dealer Manhasset Ford when new for use as a demonstrator before going to its first private owner. He owned it for a couple of years, then advertised it for sale. The owner of a wrecking yard answered the ad and, during the test drive, pulled a gun and stole the car. Apparently, he had already bought another Cobra as an insurance write-off, and restamped the chassis number from that write-off onto his newly/illegally acquired Shelby sports car. He then sold the car to the president of the Shelby Owners Association, and in 1978 French F1 driver/Le Mans winner Didier Pironi bought it. It wasn’t until the early 1990s that the chicanery was sorted out and the car was retitled with its proper chassis number. It was restored in the 1990s and converted to 427 S/C specifications, and later scanned as the model for the 427 Cobra in the 2011 video game Forza Motorsport 4 . Mecum doesn’t have a presale estimate for it, but Bonhams sold this storied Cobra five years ago for $1,050,000 . 1935 Duesenberg Model JN Convertible Coupe by Rollston and Bohman & Schwartz Darin Schnabel/RM Sotheby's RM Sotheby’s, Lot 122 There are multiple Duesenbergs on offer in Monterey this year, but this one is a particularly big deal. Actor Clark Gable ordered it new, but the Hollywood man didn’t just pick from a catalog and write a check. The car started out with coachwork from Rollston in New York City, but Gable had it sent directly to Bohman & Schwartz in California, sketched out what he wanted his new Duesenberg to look like, and worked with Bohman & Schwartz’s staff designer to make it a reality. Darin Schnabel/RM Sotheby's Darin Schnabel/RM Sotheby's Gable reportedly enjoyed the car very much, but by the late 1940s it was in New Mexico, and in 1951 it sold to a professional wrestler. It was restored in the 1970s, and in the 1980s was part of the famous Blackhawk Collection. It joined the Sam and Emily Mann collection in 2005 and immediately received another restoration followed by a slew of concours appearances. For Monterey, the bespoke Clark Gable Duesenberg has a $5.75M–$8M estimate. 1960 Chevrolet Corvette LM Kegun Morkin/RM Sotheby's RM Sotheby’s, Lot 353 In the 1950s, America’s biggest representative at Le Mans was wealthy businessman and sportsman Briggs Cunningham. He fielded a pair of modified Cadillacs there in 1950, and from 1951–55 entered cars built by his own B.S. Cunningham Company, piloted by American drivers. There were some successes, but an overall win at Le Mans eluded Cunningham, and he stopped building his own cars after 1955. He didn’t give up on racing, however, and his team instead pivoted to racing sports cars from other manufacturers like Jaguar and Maserati. For Le Mans in 1960, Cunningham returned with a team of three Corvettes, aided by unofficial support from the factory and equipped with special-order features like a temperature-controlled radiator fan, quick-ratio steering, close-ratio gearbox, Positraction differential, heavy-duty suspension, heavy-duty brake linings, heavy-duty brakes, and race-spec fuel-injected engines. Kegun Morkin/RM Sotheby's Darin Schnabel/RM Sotheby's This car is one of the three, given #1 for the race. Driving duties were supposed to fall to Briggs Cunningham and Zora Arkus-Duntov, but Arkus-Duntov, a GM employee, was ordered not to compete and Cunningham brought in American Bill Kimberly (of the Kimberly-Clark fortune) as a backup. Cunningham started the race in the car and ran as high as 21st before handing the wheel over to Kimberly, who soon met with a sudden burst of rain and rolled the car, forcing its retirement. Of the Cunningham team’s other two Corvettes, one DNF’d but another finished eighth overall and first in class. All three were sold on, and this one fell off the radar for years, only to resurface in the early 2010s in modified and neglected condition. In 2021, it was reportedly reacquired by the Cunningham family (RM Sotheby’s sold it for $758,500 that year) and restored back to its 1960 Le Mans appearance and specs, which cost over half a million dollars. Its estimate in 2026 is $2M–$2.5M. 1963 Chevrolet Corvette Grand Sport Genau AutoWerks Ingo Schmoldt/RM Sotheby's RM Sotheby’s, Lot 341 Among the most mythical Corvettes of all are the five original Grand Sports, constructed to race against and beat Shelby’s Cobra in top-level sports car racing. The last time a real Grand Sport hit the public was way back in 2009, when one of the roadsters hit a $4.9M high bid but went home unsold. When the all-new, second-generation Corvette arrived for 1963 , it brought all kinds of improvements over its predecessor. But on track, and despite the potent Z06 competition package, it often couldn’t quite keep up with the significantly lighter Cobra. Zora Arkus-Duntov, the engineering force behind Corvette performance, created the Grand Sport to alleviate the car’s weight problem. The changes to the Grand Sport were extensive, including a new lightweight chassis, extensive use of alloy components throughout, disc brakes (production Corvettes used drums until ’65), different suspension, thinner fiberglass for the body, and Plexiglas side and rear windows. The result was weight savings of well over 1000 pounds from a normal Corvette street car. The Grand Sports showed up for testing at Sebring in late 1962 and showed great promise, but word soon reached the corporate bigwigs at GM, who were still honoring the company’s ban on factory racing efforts. That a few Chevrolet engineers had quietly built a factory race car was in direct violation of that policy, and the program was canceled. Instead of throwing his hands up, though, Arkus-Duntov schemed to loan the Grand Sports to private teams and support them unofficially. Genau AutoWerks Ingo Schmoldt/RM Sotheby's Genau AutoWerks Ingo Schmoldt/RM Sotheby's Genau AutoWerks Ingo Schmoldt/RM Sotheby's This car, Chassis 003, was entrusted to Illinois Chevrolet dealer Dick Doane, who campaigned it in the Sports Car Club of America’s (SCCA) C-Modified class, as the Grand Sports were so heavily altered from stock they weren’t eligible for production-based race classes. Despite competing against purpose-built machinery, Doane earned multiple class victories in the 1963 race season. Later that year, 003 went back to Chevrolet Engineering in preparation for that year’s races at Bahamas Speed Week, and Arkus-Duntov entrusted Texan racer John Mecom to take it and two other Grand Sports to Nassau for the event. The Grand Sports now sported aluminum 377-cubic-inch V-8s fed through four Weber carburetors, and 003 qualified in third overall for the first race with Jim Hall behind the wheel, but all three Grand Sports retired with overheating issues. In the next day’s race, Augie Pabst wheeled 003 to fourth overall. In the finale, the Nassau Trophy race, 003 finished second in class and eighth overall, while another Grand Sport took class victory. More importantly, the Grand Sports proved faster than the Cobras, but after the event GM reiterated its ban on factory racing and the Grand Sport’s days were numbered. Mecom entered 003 in the 1964 Sebring 12-hour race, with John Cannon and a young A.J. Foyt driving. Foyt started the race from 62nd position but was in the top 10 within the early hours before ending up in 23rd overall and second in class at the finish. By early 1965, the car was officially in private hands, now powered by a new 427-cubic-inch V-8, and entered by Texan Alan Sevadjian for Sebring, where it finished third in class. In the 2000s, it was restored to its original 1964 Sebring specifications at a reported cost of nearly $1M, and its current output is estimated at roughly 600 hp and 600 lb-ft. For Monterey, its estimate is $11M–$13M. If it sells, it will be the most expensive Corvette ever sold at auction, and indeed the first one to break eight figures in a public sale. 1964 Shelby Cobra Daytona Coupe Gooding Christie's Gooding Christie's Gooding Christie’s, Lot 39 When Carroll Shelby famously combined the lightweight British AC Ace chassis with Ford V-8 power, his Cobras found success very quickly in American road racing. The Ace’s body wasn’t particularly slippery, though, and on some of the high-speed European circuits where Ferrari and its 250 GTO reigned supreme, the aerodynamics put Shelby at a disadvantage. So, he tasked engineer Pete Brock to come up with a coupe version of the Cobra. The so-called “Daytona Coupe,” complete with sloping fastback roof and Kamm tail, was what he came up with. And it worked, as Shelby secured a World Sportscar Championship title in 1965 thanks to the Daytona Coupe and won their class at Sebring, Daytona, Le Mans, Monza, Reims, and the Nürburgring. Gooding Christie's Gooding Christie's Gooding Christie's Chassis CSX2300, the car on offer at Pebble Beach, is the third of just six original Daytona Coupes. Its first race was the 1964 Tour de France Automobile, a grueling multi-event competition on circuits, hill climbs, and public roads. Bob Bondurant and Jochen Neerpasch drove it, winning the first two stages before various mechanical maladies kept it from overall success. The next season, CSX2300 went to Daytona, where it qualified fifth and finished sixth overall and third in class. The next month at Sebring, it stalled a few feet after starting and was rear-ended by a Volvo, but went on to finish 13th overall and third in class, setting a class lap record in the process. After Sebring, it went to Europe and got fresh white paint with blue and red stripes to represent Ford of France. Driven by Jo Schlesser and André Simon, it finished 12th overall and third in class at the Nürburgring. At the Reims 12-hour race, it was back in Shelby’s signature Guardsman Blue with Englishmen Jack Sears and John Whitmore driving, and they brought it home in ninth overall and second in class. With Shelby shifting focus to the GT40 program, CSX2300 sold into private ownership, and in 1966 it was already in Japan, where it snatched overall victories at Suzuka and Fuji. By the late ’60s it was no longer a top-level competitor on track, and it sold to a young Cobra enthusiast in Tokyo who registered it for road use, installed a milder Ford V-8, and used it regularly on the street. By the mid-1970s it was back in the U.S., and sold to Carroll Shelby himself, who had it restored and kept it until the late 1990s. It was restored again in the 2000s. With its Ferrari-beating, World Championship-winning history combined with extreme rarity, the Shelby Daytona Coupe is one of the most sought-after sports cars made in America or anywhere. The last public sale of one was in 2009, when CSX2601 sold for $7.25M, then the highest price paid for an American car at a public auction. CSX2300 could take that record back for the Daytona Coupe in 2026, as Gooding Christie’s presale estimate is “in excess of $25,000,000.” The post Red, White, and Blue-Chip: 7 Significant American Cars Selling in Monterey appeared first on Hagerty Media .

title: AFC Announces Financial Results for the Second Quarter 2026
summary: Second quarter 2026 GAAP net investment income (“NII”) of $3.5 million, or $0.15 per weighted average share WEST PALM BEACH, Fla., Aug. 13, 2026 (GLOBE...
body_text: Second quarter 2026 GAAP net investment income (“NII”) of $3.5 million, or $0.15 per weighted average share WEST PALM BEACH, Fla., Aug. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Advanced Flower Capital Inc. (Nasdaq: AFCG) (“AFC,” or the “Company”) today announced its financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. Second Quarter 2026 Highlights Total investment income of $8.7 million and GAAP NII of $3.5 million, or $0.15 per weighted average share Net asset value (“NAV”) per share of $8.25 as of June 30, 2026, compared with $7.90 as of March 31, 2026 GAAP net increase in net assets resulting from operations of $5.4 million, or $0.23 per weighted average share Gross and net investment fundings of $17.2 million and $8.0 million, respectively Investment portfolio of $289.8 million at fair value across 17 portfolio companies, compared with $279.2 million as of March 31, 2026 Weighted average yield on income producing debt investments of 13.2% as of June 30, 2026 Debt-to-equity of 1.10x and net debt-to-equity of 0.53x; total available liquidity of over $70 million Repurchased 839,406 shares at a weighted average price of $3.29, generating $0.17 per share of NAV accretion in connection with our recently adopted Share Repurchase Program (as defined below) “AFC generated net investment income of $0.15 per weighted average share in the second quarter. NAV per share increased to $8.25, including $0.17 of accretion from repurchasing shares at a substantial discount to NAV. We remained selective in the attractive lower middle-market and will continue to prioritize credit quality and risk-adjusted returns,” said Dan Neville, Chief Executive Officer. Common Stock Distribution On July 15, 2026, the Company paid a regular cash distribution of $0.05 per common share for the second quarter of 2026 to shareholders of record as of June 30, 2026. Share Repurchase Program On May 4, 2026, the Company’s Board of Directors (the “Board”) authorized a program for the purpose of repurchasing up to $5.0 million of the Company's common stock (the “Repurchase Program”). Under the Repurchase Program, the Company may, but is not obligated to, repurchase its outstanding common stock in the open market from time to time, subject to certain limitations and applicable law. Unless amended or extended by the Company's Board, the Company expects the Repurchase Program to be in place until the earlier of such time that $5.0 million of the Company's outstanding shares of common stock have been repurchased, or May 4, 2027. During the quarter, AFC repurchased and extinguished 839,406 shares at a weighted average price of $3.29, or approximately $2.8 million in the aggregate, generating $0.17 per share of NAV accretion. Amounts may not sum due to rounding. Portfolio and Investment Activity As of June 30, 2026, AFC’s investment portfolio had a fair value of $289.8 million across 17 portfolio companies in 4 industries, compared with $279.2 million across 15 portfolio companies as of March 31, 2026. Senior secured first lien debt investments represented 100% of the portfolio at fair value. During the second quarter, AFC funded $17.2 million, including $5.1 million to two new portfolio companies and $12.1 million to two existing portfolio companies. Net fundings were $8.0 million after $9.2 million of repayments, amortization, and sale proceeds. Liquidity and Capital Resources As of June 30, 2026, AFC had $207.0 million of debt outstanding, including $110.0 million under its secured revolving credit facility, $20.0 million under its unsecured revolving credit facility with an affiliate, and $77.0 million of senior unsecured notes. The weighted average interest rate on debt outstanding was 6.3% for the quarter. Debt-to-equity was 1.10x as of June 30, 2026, compared with 1.09x as of March 31, 2026. Net debt-to-equity was 0.53x, compared with 0.48x. Asset coverage was 190%, compared with 191%. Additional Information AFC issued a presentation of its second quarter 2026 results, titled “Second Quarter 2026 Earnings Presentation,” which can be viewed on the Investor Relations section of AFC’s website found here AFC -- Investor Relations . The Company also filed its Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “SEC”) on August 13, 2026. The complete webcast will be archived for 90 days on the Investor Relations section of AFC’s website. AFC distributes its earnings releases via its website and email lists. Those interested in receiving firm updates by email can sign up for them here . About AFC AFC (Nasdaq: AFCG) is a publicly traded business development company that provides flexible credit solutions to lower middle-market companies. The company primarily originates, structures, invests and manages direct senior debt investments, targeting companies generating annual EBITDA of $5 to $50 million. The company seeks to maximize risk-adjusted returns for its stockholders with an opportunistic approach across all industries. AFC is headquartered in West Palm Beach, Florida.
